title: US boosts drone surveillance as flesh-eating screwworms spread in Texas
gist: At least 200 DHS drones have been redeployed from border surveillance to thermal-imaging screwworm detection across South Texas — over 1,000 flights and 22,000 animals surveyed against 45 confirmed animal cases — while USDA races to stand up sterile-fly production at Moore Air Base by April 2027 and in Douglas, Arizona.

insights.claim: At least 200 Department of Homeland Security drones were switched from border surveillance to animal-health surveillance this summer, a reallocation of federal security hardware to an agricultural mission.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Border-security drone fleets are becoming dual-use civil infrastructure — an expanding, budget-insulated demand channel for drone and sensor vendors.
insights.quote: The effort involves at least 200 drones owned by the Department of Homeland Security, which includes the Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agency.
insights.locator: Hundreds of US government drones have switched

insights.claim: The Skydio X10 quadcopter is the primary platform, chosen for a thermal imaging sensor that can pick up elevated body temperature in animals with fevers from secondary bacterial infections caused by screwworm infestation.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A named platform winning a federal agricultural surveillance program is a concrete revenue signal for Skydio and for thermal sensor suppliers in the ag-tech stack.
insights.quote: The main drone featured in the animal health surveillance campaign appears to be the Skydio X10 quadcopter, which carries a thermal imaging sensor capable of detecting temperature differences.
insights.locator: How drone surveillance of animals works

insights.claim: Operational effectiveness depends on timing physics: crews fly shortly after sunrise because the cooler ground gives infrared sensors better contrast against warm-blooded animals.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
entities: Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
insights.so_what: Thermal detection has a narrow daily operating window, which caps daily coverage per drone and is the real constraint on scaling this program.
insights.quote: That is because the early morning work hours made it easier for the drone’s infrared sensors to detect warm-blooded animals against the relatively cooler ground.

insights.claim: Beyond thermal signatures, operators use high-resolution color imagery to spot open sores and behavioral anomalies such as 'loner' animals, and USDA is researching AI to analyze drone imagery to detect wounds, identify animals and prioritize inspections.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
entities: Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
insights.so_what: Government-funded computer vision for livestock health is an emerging procurement line that will pull ag-AI vendors into federal contracting.
insights.quote: analyze drone imagery to detect wounds, identify animals and prioritize inspections
insights.locator: The USDA is currently researching ways to use AI

insights.claim: USDA reports more than 1,000 drone flights surveying more than 22,000 animals, yet it remains unclear whether any of those flights actually produced a screwworm detection — the program's efficacy is undocumented.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Large activity metrics with no reported hit rate is the classic pattern of a program justified by optics; treat headline flight counts as spending signal, not effectiveness signal.
insights.quote: However, it’s unclear if any of the drone flights may have led to detections of animals infested by screwworms in the United States.
insights.locator: The USDA has described performing more than 1,000 drone flights

insights.claim: As of August 12 the USDA dashboard showed 45 confirmed cases in domesticated animals across South Texas and New Mexico, mostly cattle or sheep plus several dogs and a goat, since the first US detections in June.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: 45 confirmed cases is a small base with a short doubling history — the number to track weekly, since livestock trade restrictions key off case counts, not flight counts.
insights.quote: The USDA dashboard showed 45 confirmed cases in domesticated animals across South Texas and New Mexico as of August 12.
insights.locator: However, it’s unclear if any of the drone flights

insights.claim: The surveillance stack extends beyond drones to stationary trail cameras generating more than 26,000 animal observations and more than 8,000 fly traps — yet the fly traps have produced zero screwworm detections despite confirmed animal cases.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Zero trap detections alongside 45 animal cases means either trap placement or trap sensitivity is failing — a blind spot that undercuts confidence in the whole early-warning system.
insights.quote: It has also established and monitored more than 8,000 fly traps—although there have been no fly trap detections related to screwworm despite the recorded animal cases in the United States.
insights.locator: Besides using drones for aerial surveillance

insights.claim: USDA explicitly positions drones as a force multiplier for surveying more animals over rough terrain, not a substitute for the Sterile Insect Technique that remains the only proven eradication method.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Detection technology is complementary spend; the actual eradication budget flows to biological production facilities, which is where the durable capital commitment sits.

insights.claim: The US jointly funds a Panama facility releasing about 100 million sterile flies per week and began releasing a similar weekly volume in Mexico after a $21 million fruit fly facility renovation completed in June.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Roughly 200 million sterile flies a week is the current continental production baseline; any shortfall against northward spread is the metric that determines whether US livestock restrictions escalate.
insights.quote: the USDA jointly funds and manages a sterile fly production facility with Panama that releases about 100 million sterile flies each week

insights.claim: USDA is building a new sterile fly production facility at Moore Air Base in South Texas with the Army Corps of Engineers, scheduled for completion by April 1, 2027, per Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A April 2027 completion date leaves roughly eighteen months of exposure with only imported sterile flies — the window in which US cattle supply risk is highest.
insights.quote: Rollins said that the facility is scheduled for completion by April 1, 2027
insights.locator: Now that US screwworm cases have appeared

insights.claim: On July 29 USDA committed a further $25 million to a separate sterile fly facility in Douglas, Arizona, with construction potentially finished in as little as several months — a much faster timeline than the Texas facility.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Two facilities on divergent timelines suggests hedging against Texas delays; the Arizona site is the near-term capacity swing factor to monitor.
insights.quote: the USDA was providing $25 million to build a separate sterile fly facility in Douglas, Arizona

insights.claim: The Sterile Insect Technique had previously pushed screwworm south of the Darién Gap at the Panama-Colombia border, but the flies breached that barrier in 2022 and have been moving north ever since, arriving in US livestock this year.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A four-year march from the Darién Gap to Texas sets the observed spread rate; extrapolating it northward gives the timeline for broader US cattle-belt exposure.
insights.quote: But the screwworm flies breached the barrier in 2022 and have made their way northward, eventually leading to the new US cases in animals this year.
insights.locator: That method, called Sterile Insect Technique

insights.claim: The primary US exposure today is the livestock industry, but Mexico has recorded over 500 human cases across 2025 and 2026 with a recent study suggesting the infestation rate is accelerating.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: An accelerating human case curve immediately south of the border is the leading indicator that this shifts from an agricultural cost story to a public health story.
insights.quote: But Mexico has already seen over 500 human cases in 2025 and 2026, with a recent study suggesting that the infestation rate is accelerating.
insights.locator: The biggest threat that screwworm poses in the US
